label: June 2026 PYQ variants — Probability and distributions

items.stem: The only discrete distribution possessing the memoryless property is:
items.explanation: The geometric distribution is the discrete memoryless distribution: the probability of waiting at least s+t trials, conditional on already waiting s, equals the probability of waiting t more trials.

items.stem: For a Poisson distribution, mean and variance are:
items.explanation: For X~Poisson(λ), E(X)=λ and Var(X)=λ. The equality of mean and variance is a defining property of the Poisson distribution.

items.stem: For a binomial distribution, the variance is:
items.explanation: For X~Binomial(n,p), Var(X)=np(1−p)=npq. Since 0<p<1 gives q<1, the variance is smaller than the mean np.

items.stem: The negative binomial with r = 1 becomes:
items.explanation: A negative-binomial variable counts trials or failures until r successes. When r=1, it describes the number of trials until the first success, which is geometric.

items.stem: If X ~ B(n, p) with n → ∞, p → 0 and np = λ, the limiting distribution is:
items.explanation: The binomial-to-Poisson limit applies when n→∞, p→0 and np→λ. Under these conditions Binomial(n,p) converges in distribution to Poisson(λ).

items.stem: The mean of a geometric distribution with parameter p (counting trials) is:
items.explanation: For a geometric variable counting the trial on which the first success occurs, P(X=k)=(1−p)^(k−1)p and E(X)=1/p.

items.stem: X₁ ~ Poisson(2), X₂ ~ Poisson(3), independent. Then X₁ + X₂ follows:
items.explanation: Poisson is closed under independent addition

items.stem: Sampling n items without replacement from a finite population and counting successes gives:
items.explanation: Sampling without replacement from a finite population with a fixed number of successes gives a hypergeometric count. The draws are dependent, unlike binomial sampling.

items.stem: The mgf of a binomial B(n, p) is:
items.explanation: For X~Binomial(n,p), independence of the Bernoulli trials gives M_X(t)=[(1−p)+pe^t]^n=(q+pe^t)^n.

items.stem: For the negative binomial, the variance relative to the mean is:
items.explanation: rq/p² > rq/p since p < 1 — this is why it is used for overdispersed count data

items.stem: For a sample of size 4 from U(0, 1), E(X₍₂₎) is:
items.explanation: For a sample of size n from U(0,1), E[X₍ᵣ₎]=r/(n+1). With r=2 and n=4, the expectation is 2/5.

items.stem: For a sample of size n from U(0, 1), the rᵗʰ order statistic follows:
items.explanation: For n iid Uniform(0,1) observations, the r-th order statistic has a Beta distribution with shape parameters r and n−r+1.

items.stem: For a sample of size 5 from U(0, 1), E(X₍₅₎) is:
items.explanation: For U(0,1), the expected r-th order statistic is r/(n+1). The maximum is r=n, so E[X₍₅₎]=5/6.

items.stem: The cdf of the largest order statistic X₍ₙ₎ is:
items.explanation: The maximum is at most x exactly when every observation is at most x. By independence, P(X₍ₙ₎≤x)=F(x)^n.

items.stem: For an exponential population with pdf e^(−x), the cdf of X₍₇₎ in a sample of size 7 is:
items.explanation: For the unit-rate exponential, F(x)=1−e^(−x) for x≥0. The maximum of seven iid observations therefore has cdf [1−e^(−x)]⁷.

items.stem: For a sample of size n from exponential with mean θ, X₍₁₎ has mean:
items.explanation: The minimum of n iid exponential variables with mean θ has rate n/θ. Its mean is the reciprocal rate, θ/n.

items.stem: For a sample from any distribution symmetric about μ, the sample median has expectation:
items.explanation: For an odd sample size from a distribution symmetric about μ, the sample median has a distribution symmetric about μ. Provided its expectation exists, its expected value is μ.

items.stem: The expected value of the sample range from U(0, 1) with n observations is:
items.explanation: n/(n+1) − 1/(n+1). powerful simultaneously against every θ in H₁. • Against θ > θ₀, the most powerful test rejects for small values of ΣXᵢ (large θ means small observations, since the mean is 1/θ). • Against θ < θ₀, the most powerful test rejects for large values of ΣXᵢ

items.stem: The joint density of all n order statistics from a continuous distribution is:
items.explanation: (1/2θ₀)χ²₁₋α/₂,₂ₙ ≤ ΣXᵢ ≤ (1/2θ₀)χ²α/₂,₂ₙ

If X, Y are iid exponential(λ), then X/(X + Y) follows:
items.explanation: The same cancellation as in the main question

items.stem: The sum of n iid exponential(λ) variables follows:
items.explanation: The sum of n independent exponential(rate λ) variables is Gamma with shape n and rate λ. Its mean is n/λ.

items.stem: The minimum of n iid exponential(λ) variables follows:
items.explanation: The survival probability of the minimum is P(X₍₁₎>t)=P(X₁>t,…,Xₙ>t)=e^(−nλt), so the minimum is exponential with rate nλ.

items.stem: If N₁(t) and N₂(t) are independent Poisson processes with rates λ and 2λ, then P(N₁ = 1 | N₁ + N₂ = 4) equals:
items.explanation: Conditional on the total count N₁+N₂=4, the four arrivals are allocated between the independent processes with probabilities proportional to their rates. Thus N₁|total=4~Binomial(4,1/3), and P(N₁=1)=4(1/3)(2/3)³=32/81.

items.stem: The only continuous distribution with the memoryless property is:
items.explanation: The exponential distribution is the only continuous distribution on the non-negative half-line with the memoryless property P(X>s+t|X>s)=P(X>t).

items.stem: If X ~ exponential(λ), then 2λX follows:
items.explanation: If X has rate λ, then 2λX has the same distribution as the square of a standard normal variable, namely χ² with 2 degrees of freedom.

items.stem: Given X + Y = s for iid exponentials, E(X | X + Y = s) equals:
items.explanation: The mean of Uniform(0, s)

items.stem: If X ~ Binomial(m, p) and Y ~ Binomial(n, p) independent, then X | (X + Y = k) follows:
items.explanation: Condition on X+Y=k. The k successes are distributed among m trials from X and n trials from Y; the conditional count X is Hypergeometric(N=m+n, K=m, draws=k).

items.stem: The cdf of the maximum of n iid observations with common cdf F is:
items.explanation: The maximum is no greater than x only if all n observations are no greater than x. Independence gives P(X₍ₙ₎≤x)=F(x)^n.

items.stem: The cdf of the minimum of n iid observations is:
items.explanation: The minimum exceeds x only if all observations exceed x, with probability [1−F(x)]^n. Taking the complement gives F₍₁₎(x)=1−[1−F(x)]^n.

items.stem: For n iid exponential(λ) variables, the minimum follows:
items.explanation: For independent exponential(rate λ) observations, P(X₍₁₎>t)=e^(−nλt). Therefore the minimum has exponential rate nλ.

items.stem: The pdf of the maximum is:
items.explanation: Differentiate the maximum cdf F(x)^n with respect to x. The pdf is nF(x)^(n−1)f(x).

items.stem: For a sample of size n from U(0, θ), the MLE of θ is:
items.explanation: For a Uniform(0,θ) sample, the likelihood is θ^(−n) for θ≥X₍ₙ₎ and zero otherwise. It is maximised at the smallest admissible θ, namely X₍ₙ₎.

items.stem: In question 5, the UMVUE of θ is:
items.explanation: The MLE is biased downward by a factor n/(n+1)

items.stem: For a sample of size n from exponential with mean θ, E(X₍ₙ₎) equals:
items.explanation: For an exponential distribution with mean θ, E[X₍ₙ₎]=θ(1+1/2+⋯+1/n)=θHₙ, the harmonic-number multiple of θ.

items.stem: A function proposed as a cdf must satisfy, at the lower end of the support:
items.explanation: Use this to discard impossible options quickly

items.stem: For a sample of size 5 from U(0, 1), P(X₍₅₎ ≤ 0.5) equals:
items.explanation: P(X₍₅₎≤0.5)=P(all five observations are at most 0.5)=(0.5)^5=1/32.

items.stem: The joint pdf of X₍₁₎ and X₍ₙ₎ involves the factor:
items.explanation: n(n−1)[F(y) − F(x)]^(n−2)f(x)f(y) for x < y

items.stem: If A and B are independent with P(A) = 0.3 and P(B) = 0.4, then P(A ∪ B) is:
For n independent events each with probability p, P(at least one) is:
items.explanation: The complement of 'at least one occurs' is 'none occurs'. Independence gives P(none)=(1−p)^n, so the required probability is 1−(1−p)^n.

items.stem: 1 + 2 + … + n equals:
items.explanation: Pair the first and last terms, or use the arithmetic-series formula: 1+2+⋯+n=n(n+1)/2.

items.stem: If A and B are independent, then A and Bᶜ are:
items.explanation: P(A∩Bᶜ)=P(A)−P(A∩B)=P(A)−P(A)P(B)=P(A)[1−P(B)]=P(A)P(Bᶜ). Hence A and Bᶜ are independent.

items.stem: For 3 independent events with probabilities 1/2, 3/4, 7/8, P(at least one) equals:
The Bonferroni upper bound for P(∪Aᵢ) is:
items.explanation: By the union bound (first Bonferroni inequality), P(∪ᵢAᵢ)≤ΣᵢP(Aᵢ).

items.stem: The law of total variance states Var(Y) equals:
items.explanation: The law of total variance is Var(Y)=E[Var(Y|X)]+Var(E[Y|X]). It separates average conditional variation from variation in the conditional mean.

items.stem: If Y | X ~ Poisson(X), then E(Y) equals:
items.explanation: For Y|X~Poisson(X), E(Y|X)=X. Taking expectations again gives E(Y)=E[X].

items.stem: A Poisson distribution mixed over a Gamma-distributed mean gives:
items.explanation: A Poisson distribution with a Gamma-distributed random mean produces a negative-binomial marginal distribution. This is the Poisson–Gamma mixture.

items.stem: For an exponential distribution with mean 1/λ, the variance is:
items.explanation: An exponential distribution with rate λ has mean 1/λ and variance 1/λ².

items.stem: For any mixture of Poisson distributions, the variance is:
E(Y | X) is:
options: a random variable that is a function of X
items.explanation: The conditional expectation E(Y|X) is measurable with respect to X; it is a function of the information contained in X and is therefore a random variable.

items.stem: If X and Y are independent, E(Y | X) equals:
items.explanation: If X and Y are independent, conditioning on X does not change the distribution or expectation of Y. Thus E(Y|X)=E(Y).

items.stem: If Y | X ~ Binomial(n, X) with X ~ Beta(a, b), then Y follows:
items.explanation: Mixing a Binomial(n,p) distribution over p~Beta(a,b) gives a Beta-binomial distribution.

items.stem: If Y | X ~ N(X, 1) and X ~ N(0, σ²), then Var(Y) equals:
items.explanation: E[Var] + Var[E] = 1 + σ²

items.stem: Under ρ = 0, the exact test statistic for H₀: ρ = 0 is:
items.explanation: Under bivariate normal sampling and H₀:ρ=0, the statistic t=r√(n−2)/√(1−r²) follows Student's t distribution with n−2 degrees of freedom.

items.stem: For n = 4 and ρ = 0, the distribution of r is:
items.explanation: When n=4 and ρ=0, the exact density of the sample correlation coefficient is constant on (−1,1), so r is Uniform(−1,1).

items.stem: For n = 3 and ρ = 0, the distribution of r is:
items.explanation: For n=3 and ρ=0, the sample correlation density is proportional to (1−r²)^(−1/2), which is the U-shaped arcsine distribution on (−1,1).

items.stem: Fisher’s z transformation of r is:
items.explanation: Fisher's transformation is z=atanh(r)=½ log[(1+r)/(1−r)]. It maps correlations in (−1,1) to the real line.

items.stem: The approximate variance of Fisher’s z is:
items.explanation: and importantly it does not depend on ρ

items.stem: As ρ approaches 1, the distribution of r becomes:
items.explanation: As the population correlation approaches 1, the sample correlation distribution becomes increasingly concentrated near the upper boundary and increasingly asymmetric.

items.stem: If ρ = 1 exactly, the distribution of r is:
items.explanation: If the population correlation is exactly 1 in a non-degenerate bivariate normal model, the sample correlation is 1 with probability one. Its distribution is a point mass at 1.

items.stem: r = 0 implies:
items.explanation: A sample correlation of zero means there is no linear sample association. It does not in general imply independence; that implication needs additional assumptions such as joint normality.

items.stem: The sample correlation r relates to the two regression slopes by:
items.explanation: The product of the two simple-regression slopes equals r². Since b_yx=r(s_y/s_x) and b_xy=r(s_x/s_y), their product is r².

items.stem: Fisher’s z is preferred over the t test when testing:
items.explanation: The t test handles only the null value zero

items.stem: For a Poisson process with rate 2 per minute, P(interarrival time > 6 | > 4) equals:
items.explanation: The exponential interarrival time is memoryless. P(T>6|T>4)=P(T>2)=e^(−2×2)=e^(−4).

items.stem: If A and B are mutually exclusive with positive probabilities, they are:
items.explanation: If A and B are mutually exclusive, P(A∩B)=0. If both have positive probabilities, P(A)P(B)>0, so the independence condition fails; they are dependent.

items.stem: For a convex function g, Jensen’s inequality states:
items.explanation: Jensen's inequality for a convex function g states E[g(X)]≥g(E[X]), whenever the expectations exist.

items.stem: For a positive random variable X, E(1/X) compared with 1/E(X) is:
items.explanation: The function g(x)=1/x is convex for x>0 because g″(x)=2/x³>0. Jensen's inequality therefore gives E(1/X)≥1/E(X).

items.stem: For a non-negative random variable, E(X) equals:
items.explanation: For a non-negative random variable, the tail-integral identity is E(X)=∫₀∞P(X>x)dx=∫₀∞[1−F(x)]dx.

items.stem: E(X²) for non-negative X equals:
items.explanation: Step 1 — X₍₇₎ in a sample of size 7 is the maximum. Step 2 — the maximum’s cdf is the product of the individual cdfs. F₍ₙ₎(x) = P(X₍ₙ₎ ≤ x) = P(all n observations ≤ x) = ∏P(Xᵢ ≤ x) = [F(x)]ⁿ using independence

items.stem: Markov’s inequality states that for X ≥ 0:
items.explanation: Step 3 — write F for the exponential. With f(x) = e^(−x) (rate 1)

items.stem: Chebyshev’s inequality bounds P(|X − μ| ≥ 2σ) by:
items.explanation: Chebyshev's inequality gives P(|X−μ|≥kσ)≤1/k². Setting k=2 yields the upper bound 1/4.

items.stem: E(log X) ≤ log E(X) holds because log is:
items.explanation: The logarithm is concave on (0,∞), so Jensen's inequality reverses the convex-function direction: E[log X]≤log E[X].

items.stem: Var(X) ≥ 0 is a special case of Jensen’s inequality applied to:
items.explanation: The function g(x)=x² is convex. Jensen gives E(X²)≥[E(X)]², which is equivalent to Var(X)≥0.

items.stem: For a discrete non-negative integer-valued X, E(X) equals:
items.explanation: For a non-negative integer-valued variable, the tail-sum formula is E(X)=Σₖ₌₀∞P(X>k).

items.stem: The Cauchy–Schwarz inequality applied to random variables yields:
items.explanation: Cauchy–Schwarz gives |E(XY)|²≤E(X²)E(Y²). Applied to centred, standardised variables, this yields |Corr(X,Y)|≤1.

items.stem: For an iid sample of size n from an exponential distribution with mean θ, the expected value of the minimum order statistic X₍₁₎ is:
items.explanation: The minimum of n independent exponential variables with mean θ is exponential with rate n/θ, so its mean is θ/n.

items.stem: For an iid exponential sample with mean θ, which estimator is unbiased for θ?
items.explanation: Since E[X₍₁₎]=θ/n, multiplying the minimum by n gives E[nX₍₁₎]=θ.

items.stem: Let X and Y be independent exponential random variables with the same rate. Conditional on X+Y=s, the density of X is:
items.explanation: The joint density is proportional to exp(−λx)exp(−λ(s−x))=exp(−λs), constant for 0<x<s. Normalising gives the Uniform(0,s) conditional distribution.

items.stem: Independent events A₁,A₂,A₃ satisfy P(Aᵢ)=1−2⁻ⁱ. The probability that at least one occurs is:
items.explanation: By independence, P(no event occurs)=∏₂⁻ⁱ=2⁻⁽¹⁺²⁺³⁾=1/64. The required probability is the complement, 63/64.

items.stem: Suppose X is exponential with mean 2 and Y|X=x is Poisson(x). What is Var(Y)?
items.explanation: By total variance, Var(Y)=E[Var(Y|X)]+Var(E[Y|X])=E(X)+Var(X). For an exponential variable with mean 2, E(X)=2 and Var(X)=4, so Var(Y)=6.

items.stem: For an iid exponential sample with mean θ and size n, E[X₍ₙ₎] is:
items.explanation: The expected maximum of n iid exponential variables with mean θ is θHₙ, where Hₙ=1+1/2+⋯+1/n.

items.stem: For exponential observations with mean θ, the spacing X₍ᵣ₎−X₍ᵣ₋₁₎ has expectation:
items.explanation: The r-th spacing has exponential rate (n−r+1)/θ. Its expectation is therefore θ/(n−r+1).

items.stem: For 1≤r≤n, which transformation of the r-th exponential order-statistic spacing is unbiased for the mean θ?
items.explanation: The spacing has expectation θ/(n−r+1). Multiplication by n−r+1 therefore produces an estimator with expectation θ.

items.stem: For a random sample, the arithmetic mean of all n order statistics equals:
items.explanation: Ordering only rearranges the observations. Thus ΣX₍ᵢ₎=ΣXᵢ and their averages are identical; the sample mean is unbiased for θ.

items.stem: The spacings of iid exponential order statistics are:
items.explanation: The successive spacings of exponential order statistics are independent exponential variables, with rates that decrease as the order increases.

items.stem: If X₁,…,X₄ are iid exponential with mean θ, then E[X₍₁₎] is:
items.explanation: The minimum of four iid exponential variables has rate 4/θ and therefore mean θ/4.

items.stem: If the exponential distribution is parameterised by rate λ, the minimum of n iid observations has rate:
items.explanation: The survival probability of the minimum is the product of the n individual survival probabilities: e^(−nλx). Hence its rate is nλ.

items.stem: For iid exponential observations with mean θ, the sample mean X̄ is unbiased because:
items.explanation: Linearity of expectation gives E(X̄)=n⁻¹ΣE(Xᵢ)=θ, regardless of the dependence among order statistics after sorting.
